title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Organizing Spatial Data in a GIS
text:
Organizing Spatial Data in a GIS

A GIS doesn’t save information as maps

Rather, we tell the GIS how to locate objects in relation to other objects and in space

Things to be aware of:

Your spatial data model
The relationships your objects have with each other in the real world

e.g. street intersections or shared state borders
We call this “topology”

text:

Most common are vector and raster

text: Spatial Data Models

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Vector Model

Features are stored as discrete points, lines or polygons
All are combinations of nodes and/or vertices
Locations are recorded as X,Y coordinates

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Vector Model

Features are stored as discrete points, lines or polygons
All are combinations of nodes and/or vertices
Locations are recorded as X,Y coordinates

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
The Attribute Table

Each feature – point, line, or polygon – is dynamically linked to the “attribute table” or set of variables

For example, you could have a dataset of cities, represented as points, and the attribute table might contain characteristics of the city – population, for example

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Types of Feature Classes



Feature classes – or datasets of spatial objects – contain only the same types of objects

This means only points or lines or polygons
And since they all share the same attribute table, they should be the same thing

So, no combining cities and septic systems in one feature class, even though both might be points
Each group of features is referred to as a feature class

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
This is our Nation’s Capital…


…But what can we say about the type of spatial data the map shows?
Knowing whether we’re working with lines or polygons is key to understanding what types of analysis we can do.

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Why We Like the Vector Model
text:
Why We Like the Vector Model

Features can be located precisely
We can store lots of information (variables or attributes) about each feature
Useful for many types of map-making
Perfect for types of analysis, such as areas, lengths, or connections
Used a lot in the social sciences

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Raster Data Model



Sub-divides a study area into square pixels – rows and columns
Only need the location of the upper left-hand corner and all other locations are implicit, assuming you know your pixel size
Only one value is recorded for each pixel

For example, temperature, precipitation, or land use type

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Raster Data Model
So long as the x, y location is georeferenced (placed on the surface of the earth), we can locate each other pixel, too

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Raster Data Model

There are at least two contexts in which raster data may make more sense than vector data:

When you’re working with continuous data, like the types of information mentioned above: e.g. precipitation or temperature

Often, these types of information weren’t collected for administrative units, anyway, so it makes little sense to organize them that way

Applications that involve the environmental sciences (see reason 1 for a good reason why)




Remember that rasters don’t have attribute tables – each cell or pixel is only going to have one value attached to it

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Raster Data Model
Rasters can be used to represent continuous data

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Raster Data Model
Or discrete data

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Why We Like the Raster Model
text:
Why We Like the Raster Model

Best for continuous data
Analysis can sometimes be faster
And some types of analysis require raster data
Remember: pixel size (or resolution) matters!

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Vector versus raster





“Yes, raster is faster, but raster is vaster, and vector just seems more correcter.” – Dana Tomlin

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
The GIS Commandments

Thou shalt not (ever) use Windows to copy or move files! (Use Catalog)
Thou shalt not work from the Downloads folder.
Thou shalt understand how file directories are structured (even if you wish you didn’t need to).
Know your projection.
Save projects early and often!
Thou shalt google (look things up when you have questions).
Embrace mistakes (you will make mistakes).

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
ArcGIS Pro and File Types

When you do work in ArcGIS Pro, your efforts are saved as a project

Your project links to the data you’ve added, but does not actually include said data
If you copy your project to another location, without moving the individual layers as well, your project will be empty when you open it
ArcGIS Pro tries to help you out by creating a project folder and default geodatabase when you start a project

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
ArcGIS Pro and File Types

Vector data are typically stored as shapefiles or as elements of a geodatabase or geopackage, although other formats exist

Shapefiles are typically recognized by other GIS software applications and this is the term often used to refer to spatial data
Geodatabases can include feature classes, but also raster data and even spreadsheet (e.g. MS Excel) data

These look like a cylinder in ArcGIS Pro; when you expand the cylinder, you see all the data included in the geodatabase
This is an Esri proprietary file format

Geopackages are similar to geodatabases

Both shapefiles and geodatabases will look unrecognizable in Windows

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Topology – Modeling Feature Behavior

Topology sets the rules of behavior for features in a feature class
Basic topology rules deal with adjacency, connectivity, overlap, and intersection
A classic example is road networks

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
We all understand where the U.S. is:

Implicitly, we step out of Minnesota to the north and we’re in Canada
Our data need to reflect this: adjacency
One border

Or street intersections

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: It All Comes Down to Logical Consistency
text:
It All Comes Down to Logical Consistency

How well do features mimic real-world situations?
As users, rather than generators, of data, we often have no control over the quality of the data we have to work with
Many of these issues won’t be apparent if we’re only making maps, but can wreak havoc with analysis

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: How to we translate spherical locations to map locations?
text:
How to we translate spherical locations to map locations?

To do that, we need to discuss:

Characterizing the shape of the earth
Projections
Coordinate Systems

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
The shape of the earth

Obviously not flat, but not perfectly round either

More like an oblate spheroid or ellipsoid (someone sat on the top of it a bit)

And as technology has advanced, we’ve been able to be more precise about the exact shape

Now satellites, rather than just surveying

A datum is an estimate of the ellipsoid and measures the elevation of every point on earth

Recent datums use the center of the earth as the reference point, not a point on the ground
North American Datum of 1983 (NAD83) is most recent datum for the US
At large scales, differences in datum used can make a big difference

Geoids, based on science of geodesy, provide exact measurements of earth’s size and shape (and gravitational fields)

Rarely necessary in GIS

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: How do we find locations on the Earth?
text:
How do we find locations on the Earth?






Latitude: parallels, measured north and south of the equator
Longitude: meridians are like orange segments, measured against the prime meridian

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Coordinate Systems – locating a place on the surface of the earth
text:
Coordinate Systems – locating a place on the surface of the earth

Geographic Coordinates – latitude and longitude, expressed as numbers
Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) – Uses transverse Mercator projection, which is accurate in North-South strips.

Divides the earth into 60 zones.
Not used in polar regions – too much distortion

Military Grid – Uses a lettering system (CDE, 123) with 60 zones
State Plane System – Used for a lot of geographic information in the US.

Based on a different map of each state, and each state is divided into a number of zones, depending how large it is (one for RI).
Very little distortion, because of the small areas covered.
Can be a pain if you’re working with data for more than one state.

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Map Projection

Putting the round earth onto a flat surface (paper, computer screen, projector screen)
Sphere is “projected” onto plane, cone, or cylinder

Azimuthal
Conic
Cylindrical

How do these shapes intersect the earth’s surface?

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Types of Projections

Projections can be measured by how they distort the earth’s surface:

Conformal projections are shape-preserving

Lines of latitude and longitude will meet at right angles
They preserve direction and so are used in cases where measuring direction is important

Equal area or equivalent projections preserve area

Area is portrayed correctly, as on a sphere

Distance preserving projections (but only along a few lines
Compromise projections

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Orthographic
A globe!

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Mercator
Cylindrical and shape (and angle) preserving

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Gall-Peters
Cylindrical and equal-area (but shape-distorting)

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Albers Equal-Area Conic
Conic (obviously)—preserves area while distorting shape

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Lambert Conformal Conic
Conic but preserves shape (and angle)

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area
Planar (preserves area while distorting shape)

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Important to remember:

Any projection distorts either distance, shape, area, or direction. No projection is perfect
The larger the area involved, the larger the impact of map errors due to projection
Projection used should suit the GIS application
Maps must be in the same projection if they’ll be overlayed or stitched together
Usually a GIS can switch from one projection to another

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Why does this matter?




When we add data to our GIS from different sources, we need the information to “line up” nicely – so we need to know the projection and it should be the same for all layers
If the type of analysis we’re going to be doing involves area measurement or distance, for example, we want to make sure we’re using an appropriate projection.

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Types of data

Nominal – Information that names or identifies objects

Could be text or a number, but we wouldn’t do math with the number
Examples: County names or census tract numbers
Represented on a map using labels

Categorical – Information that is classified into groups, classes, or categories with no ranking involved

Again, the information could be text or a number, but we wouldn’t do math with the number
Examples: urban/rural; residential/commercial/agricultural
Represented on a map using unique value maps

Ordinal – Information is classified into groups, but there is an assumed ranking to the categories

For example: Opinion polls, income, or educational attainment
Represented on a map using either graduated color or unique value maps

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Type of Data, continued

Numeric – Information stored as numbers, with a regularly spaced measurement scale

Often continuous data, such as income or rainfall
Ratio data are numeric information with a meaningful zero value, such as no rainfall, income, or height

Doing math with these types of data makes common sense

Interval data re the same as ratio data, but do not have a meaningful zero point

Data with negative values must be interval

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Representing different kinds of information

The way in which we display data on the map needs to match not only the type of data but also the type of feature

Nominal – labels
Categorical – different symbol or color for each category
Ordinal – we want to use color or symbol size to convey the increase in value that goes with each category

Graduated or proportional symbol maps.

Numerical – for points and lines, we use lines thickness or symbol size to express variations in value

For polygons we use graduated color or choropleth maps
Single color that changes in intensity to convey changes in value
Sometimes two colors are used

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Classification Schemes

Mapping continuous data means we need a meaningful way to create categories – this is called classification
Similar to choices that are made in generating a histogram
How we allocate values to categories will affect our final map

This means number of categories
But also the classification scheme itself

Ideally you are able to justify your choices (good general advice!)

What is the takeaway message you want to convey?
Who is your audience?

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Most common types of classification

Natural breaks (Jenks) – looks at the distribution of values and sets the break points at “natural breaks” in the data
Equal interval – Creates a set number of classes of equal size
Fixed interval – Same as equal interval, except you decide the size of the interval and the number of classes depends on that decision (e.g., by 1,000s)
Quantile (equal count) – puts the same number of features into each class
Standard deviation – creates categories based on the number of standard deviations away from the mean
Manual – you choose the break points yourself

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: What do we need to think about?
text:
What do we need to think about?

Map elements – the pieces of a map that make it a finished (and polished product)

Individual elements should contribute to conveying information, not detract from it
Limit clumping together of elements
Limit use of multiple fonts and colors

Map symbology – the way in which the information the map conveys is portrayed

Colors – hue, intensity, and saturation
Symbols – size and type

By necessity, maps are selective of the information they show and information is generalized

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Choosing symbols and colors

Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, but there are some general guidelines!
Water and land should not be given unusual colors—e.g., water is blue not red
Increased thickness of lines or larger symbols should match increased value
Darker or more intense colors usually go with higher values
If you use a color ramp with two colors, your data should also reflect two extremes in value—for example, in and out migration or voting patterns
Avoid mixing and matching lots of different patterns on the same map—the eye can’t handle it

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text: Source: https://colorbrewer2.org/#type=sequential&scheme=BuGn&n=3

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Map Scale

Often referred to as the “representative fraction”

Relationship of units on the ground to map units
The fraction or ratio of objects on the page to real life objects

Common USGS scale for topographical maps is 1:24,000
1:100,000 means one centimeter on the map is equivalent to 100,000 centimeters (or 1 km) in the real world
Fitting a map of the world into two book pages requires a scale of about 1:100,000,000
Scale is unitless – we could be talking about 1 foot to 24,000 feet or 1 meter to 24,000 meters

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
What makes a “map”?

Cartographic elements:

Title
Neatline
Scale bar
Legend
North arrow
Inset map

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: So many ways to visualize information on a map!
text:
So many ways to visualize information on a map!

Thematic Maps – organize and display spatial variation of a single variable
Choropleth maps – changes in a variable are classified and mapped by some administrative category (e.g. countries or states)
Dasymetric maps – Uses additional information to allocate value within polygons
Isoline or contour maps – lines delineate areas of similar value. E.g., air pressure or elevation
Reference maps – may display lots of different types of information

Topological maps or atlases

Dot maps, picture symbol maps, graduated symbol maps
Network and flow maps – show direction and magnitude of flows
Cartograms—a unit’s display area is determined not by its actual area but by an attribute value

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Questions we can ask about maps and spatial data
text:
Questions we can ask about maps and spatial data

What are the high and low values and where are they?
Does there appear to be a relationship between location and value?
Do similar values appear to be located close together, or clustered? Is another spatial pattern discernible?
Are there characteristics of areas that appear to correspond with particular sets of values? e.g. coastal or inner city.
Would the pattern change if we change the scale of analysis? For example, what happens to the spatial pattern if we go from counties to states?

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
A definition

GISs are “automated systems for the capture, storage, retrieval, analysis, and display of spatial data.”
— Clarke, 1995



Another way of thinking about it

“GIS” is shorthand for a combination of spatial tools and applications, methods, concepts, and data that help us organize, visualize, and ask spatial questions

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
section: Some things we can do with a GIS
text:
Some things we can do with a GIS

Data visualization – for example, exploratory analysis or cartography
Explore geographic coincidence – for example, how many new firms in a region
Calculate geometries – for example, length of road in an area, or the center of a polygon
Identify spatial patterns – for example, clusters or hot spots
Find spatial relationships – for example, measuring exposure, accessibility, or market areas
Calculate spatial variables – for example, distance or proximity
Estimate values or density – for example, interpolation

Visualization
Geographic data science
AI/machine learning

Data

Data are pieces of information
Databases are forms of data organization that allow us to easily retrieve data

How the data are organized will determine what kinds of information we can retrieve about the data
Example: the phone book

Data models – logical constructs for storage and retrieval of data

Fields or attributes or variables
Records or tuples or observations

text:
Data Tables in ArcGIS Pro

These are the tables that accompany feature classes (points, lines, polygons)
Right click on layer and open table

Standalone tables

Tables that are not associated with a feature class

For example summary statistics
Or a table of data for places

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Data in a GIS environment

Spatial data model – How the spatial element of the data is organized

Vector v. raster
Information about location and topology of our points, lines, and polygons

Attribute data model – data that provide information about characteristics of the spatial features

Attribute or standalone tables

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Database management systems (DBMS)

Elements of a DBMS:

Data definition language – Allows user to set up or define new database, including numbers and types of attributes
Data dictionary – Catalog of attributes and their “legal” values and ranges
Data entry – Ways to enter new data and ensure they follow the rules laid out by the data dictionary
Verification and updating – Deleting, modifying, or inserting records and creating reports

Information can be stored in binary or ASCII format

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Field types

Databases like to have the same kind of information in a field

E.g. numbers, strings, or dates
But also information on:

Length – how many letters in a string field
Precision – how many numbers in a numerical field
Scale – the number of decimal places

Generally, once we define a field, its type cannot be changed

Generating New Fields in ArcGIS Pro

A major function of working in a GIS is the creation or generation of new information, or variables

Much of our work this semester will cover ways of generating spatial variables (e.g., distance or density)
We also create new variables based on existing variables, however

For example, percent population that is x = (total x population/total population)*100

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Types of DBMS

Flat files – simple, but not efficient
Hierarchical – inflexible relationships
Relational – multiple tables, but relationships between tables are defined as needed

Importance of the “primary key”

Object and Object-Relational – better for storing complete objects and and object behavior, but not as popular as relational databases

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Codd’s Five Database Rules

Only one value is stored at any intersection of row and column.
All values in a column deal with the same subject.
Each row is unique.
There is no significance to the sequence of rows.
There is no significance to the sequence of columns.

Attribute queries
Spatial queries

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Attribute queries

Attribute queries create a subset of records or features that meet the query criteria
Can be simple, like “Find California”

This can be done by sorting, browsing, or searching

Or selecting features that meet particular criteria (like minimum city size)
Once we’ve created our selection we can:

Generate summary statistics
Create new feature class or shapefile
Create new variables that label features as having a particular characteristic

ArcGIS uses Structured Query Language (SQL)

Common database query language
Basically a logical expression that generates a selected set of records

For example, all cities larger than 50,000 inhabitants
Or all “highly active” volcanoes
We can then “summarize” information based on our selected set of cities – e.g. median income for all cities greater than 50,000 inhabitants

In ArcGIS Pro we use Select by Attribute

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Spatial queries

Spatial queries also generate a subset of features, but not based on their attribute characteristics

Instead, we’re interested in their spatial characteristics
For example, all housing units within 500 meters of a major interstate
We call this “selecting by location”

Common types of spatial queries:

Proximity – All children within a mile of a school
Containment – All the schools in a particular county
Intersection – All the US counties that touch the coastline

Can also be features that overlap or cross features from another layer


Interactive selection – Can be done via table or map

You use the mouse to select the features you want

Buffers are often helpful

For example, rest stops and interstates

(Look at metadata!)

Export to a project geodatabase

Use “Environment” tab to select the appropriate projection to export the data in

title: Principles & Methods of Geographic Information Systems
text:
Why collect our own data?

When data on the topic we’re interested in is not available
When the variables or characteristics of a place or thing don’t exist
To have a more engaged/subjective view on a topic
To collect data at a fine spatial resolution (e.g., a bench or a sculpture)
